meta.title: AGENTS.md or a skill?
meta.goal: After this you can decide whether a piece of guidance belongs in AGENTS.md or in a skill, and say why in one sentence.

criterion.text: Get 6 of the 7 questions right, including which side a procedure belongs on.

steps.hint: Before it reads any file, the agent decides the file is worth reading. Ask yourself what it decides from.
steps.prompt: Your agent has a folder of skills installed. You are asking about something else, and none of it is the skill's job. How much of that skill is the agent holding?
options: Its name and one line saying what it is for
The whole skill file, every turn
steps.feedback: An installed skill rides along as one line: its name and the line that says what it is for. That line is what the agent matches your request against, and it is the only reason a skill can fire without you naming it. The rest of the file waits on disk until the line matches. AGENTS.md goes the other way: the whole file arrives on every turn, which is why it has to stay short.

misconception.0: A skill you have not asked for feels invisible. One line for each installed skill is in the list the agent reads at the start, and that line is what lets the skill fire on its own.
misconception.2: Only the one line is loaded. The file itself waits, and it is read only after the agent decides the skill is relevant. That split is what makes a long skill cheap while you work on something else.
misconception.default: One line per skill is in the list. The file itself waits.

steps.prompt: Where does each line belong? Drag each one onto a side.

items.text: Never push to main. Open a pull request.
Our test command is npm test, and it must pass before you commit.
How to turn a topic into a ten step practice exercise.
Cite AI-written code with an inline comment.
The palette, the type scale and the spacing tokens for design work.
Write plainly, in short sentences, with no em dashes.
The eight steps for publishing a page to GitHub Pages.
Who to email when the build breaks.

steps.feedback: A rule that has to hold on every turn goes in AGENTS.md, because a skill only arrives when the agent decides it is relevant. Guidance tied to a moment goes in a skill: the design tokens you read while doing design, the steps for publishing, who to email when a build breaks. Voice works the same way: the rules live in a skill that fires when you write prose, and at most one line of AGENTS.md says when to call it. The test is not how important a line feels. It is whether it has to be true on a turn about something else.
steps.misconception: The tempting mistake is to file by importance, so a rule you care about becomes a skill. Importance is the wrong test. Ask instead whether the line has to hold on every turn, even a turn about something unrelated.

steps.hint: Think about what every turn pays for.
steps.prompt: Your AGENTS.md has reached 900 lines, and the agent has started missing rules that sit in the middle. What is the fix?
options: Repeat the rules you care about at the top and again at the bottom
Delete the rules the agent has been ignoring, since it must not need them
Move the procedures and the reference into skills, and keep the standing rules in AGENTS.md
steps.feedback: A long instruction file does not make the agent try harder. Every line competes for attention with the line beside it, and attention is strongest at the start and the end, so the middle of a long file is where rules get lost. Move what is a procedure or a pile of reference into a skill, where it arrives only when it fires, and keep AGENTS.md for the rules that must hold every turn.

misconception.0: Repeating a rule feels like emphasis. It is a symptom: the file is carrying material that belongs in a skill, and once that leaves, the rule does not need saying twice.
misconception.1: A rule worth having does not stop being worth having because the file around it grew. Move the procedures and the reference out first, then look at what is left.
misconception.default: A long instruction file dilutes the rules inside it. Move the procedures and the reference out.

steps.prompt: Which of these should be a skill the agent may not start on its own?
options: Publish your exercise to a public web page
Wipe the local database and reseed it
Explain what a React hook is
A four step release run: research, plan, implement, review
Turn a topic into a practice exercise
steps.feedback: Two things earn it. One is a step that is hard to undo, or that has to be your call: publishing, wiping a database, rotating keys. The other is a run you start on purpose, like a four step release, where the value is that you decide when it happens. Both take the same key, and both save context: a skill with disable-model-invocation: true is not in the agent's list at all, so it costs nothing while you work on something else. Everything else is better left reachable, because a skill you have to name before it fires cannot help you while you are thinking about something else.

misconception.2: This is one to leave reachable. The moment you want it is the moment your question is unclear, which is exactly when the agent should reach for it on its own.
misconception.4: The opposite of this one: the words you would type to start it are also the words that should let it fire, so it does its job best when the agent can reach for it.
misconception.default: Hard to undo, or yours to start: both take the key.

steps.prompt: Match each problem to the move that fixes it.
lefts: A rule that must hold on every task, and it is sometimes missed
A 200 line procedure the agent needs twice a week
A skill that exists but never fires
A run of four steps you want to start yourself, like a release
rights: Make it a skill, so the cost waits until it fires
Put it in AGENTS.md, so it is there on every turn
Rewrite the description to say what it does and when to use it
steps.feedback: A rule that must always hold cannot depend on the agent noticing it, so it goes in AGENTS.md. A long procedure that matters twice a week is a skill, where its cost waits until it fires. A skill that never fires has a description problem: the description is the only part the agent reads when it decides. A run you start on purpose, or a step that is hard to undo, gets disable-model-invocation: true, which also keeps it out of the agent's list until you call for it.
steps.misconception: A rule you must never miss feels like it needs a procedure behind it, so making it a skill is tempting. But a skill fires only when the model reads your request and decides it is relevant, and a rule that has to hold every time cannot wait for that.

steps.prompt: Put the four questions in the order that decides where a piece of guidance goes.
options: Then it is a skill. Does the model need to find it on its own?
Must this hold on every single task, with no exception?
If not, add disable-model-invocation: true so a person starts it.
Is it short enough to be worth carrying on every turn?
steps.feedback: Ask first whether the line has to be true on every turn, because that decides it. If it does, no skill can promise it, since a skill fires only when the agent decides it is relevant. If it does not have to hold every turn, ask whether it is short. Short and occasional still fits in AGENTS.md. Anything longer becomes a skill, and the last question is whether the agent should be able to reach for it on its own. If it should not, that is the same switch you set for a run you want to start yourself.
steps.misconception: It is tempting to start with whether the model should find it on its own, because that is the interesting question. But it is the last one. A line that must hold on every turn never reaches it, because no skill can promise that.

steps.prompt: A rule that must hold on every task belongs in which file? Type its name.
steps.feedback: AGENTS.md is the file the session opens with, so it sits in front of the model on every turn. A skill is the other shelf: one line always, and its body only on the turn that line matches.
steps.misconception: A skill is the wrong answer here, and it is the common one. A skill is reached only when the model decides the request is relevant, so it cannot promise that a rule holds on every turn.
